report.code_assessment: The code follows the spec closely. Nearly every source file maps onto a scope, and user-visible text, keyboard shortcuts, layout and behaviour usually match the spec's wording exactly, often down to tooltips and labels. The spec defines what the application does. The code fills in how: exact pixel sizes, animation springs and timings, how often things poll, how files are stored on disk, and how the external tools (claude, piton, git) are called and their output parsed. The few real departures are small. The hidden anchor has a mode property the spec never mentions. A Markdown workaround turns inline code in replies into plain text. The diff view's module comment is out of date. A few helper modules, like fuzzy scoring, link resolution and shell formatting, apply only a short spec sentence through heuristics of their own.
report.spec_assessment: The spec is unusually complete and precise for a desktop app. Most scope files set out exact labels, keyboard shortcuts, sizes, colours, animations, persistence locations and edge cases, and the code follows them very closely: the strings, constants (e.g. 400 files, 32px inset, 260/160px sidebar, 80%/20%/95% drawer, 12 rows, 5s LSP timeout, 3 import rounds) and behaviours are carried over almost word for word, often with tests quoting the spec. What's left over is small: some wording differs (the palette's "Build Spec" instead of "Build", "None found", extra subheadings in the divergence report), git state is read separately by the tree, panel and diff view rather than from one Git scope, and a few areas (the project directory picker, the application-level file layout, the empty Code and Research tabs, the lib and agent meta-files) are thin or aren't meant to be built in src. Overall the code tracks the spec closely, with divergence mostly in small wording and structural choices rather than missing behaviour.

well_defined.why: The on-disk layout, naming, restore behaviour, auto send and what a record holds are described precisely.

well_defined.name: Chat input and Ask flow
well_defined.why: Tabs, the Chain animation, tints, help text, question stacking, the answer drawer's sizes and resizing, step collapsing, text selection and attachments are all described precisely.

well_defined.name: Scrollbar
well_defined.why: Button layout, thumb geometry, measuring rows for steadiness, lock-to-bottom rules and even the lock pulse's timing and ring scale are specified.

well_defined.name: Folder browser
well_defined.why: Every keyboard shortcut on each platform, type-to-select timing, new-folder validation and focus behaviour are given.

well_defined.name: Git panel
well_defined.why: Commit message composition, note generation constraints, pull merge/conflict semantics and feedback notifications are exact.

well_defined.name: Diff view
well_defined.why: Both layouts, line marking, context and collapse thresholds, navigation keys and loading/binary/empty states are defined.

less_defined.name: Harness process integration
less_defined.why: The spec says only one-off runs in auto mode that stream and carry on conversations, so the CLI flags, stream-json parsing, which tool argument counts as most telling, and how errors are handled are all the implementation's own.

less_defined.name: Hidden anchor format and compilation
less_defined.why: The spec names userPrompt, systemPrompt and attachedText but not the anchor's naming, how imports are written, the compile command, or how config values are read, and the code adds a mode property of its own.

less_defined.name: Visual metrics and animation
less_defined.why: Most sizes, spring constants, slide durations, tint opacities and row heights in prompt mode, the ribbon, the scrollbar and the chat input are the implementation's choices.

less_defined.name: Supporting utilities
less_defined.why: Fuzzy scoring weights, how links resolve to files, when a shell command counts as long enough to split, and the Markdown inline-code workaround come from a sentence or two of spec, or none.

less_defined.name: Refresh and file watching
less_defined.why: The spec asks for updates within a couple of seconds, and the code picks 2-second git polling, 150ms watcher batching, 100ms diagnostics collection and diff re-reads on its own.

less_defined.name: Project directory
less_defined.why: Only says a file picker selects piton.config.pi for the session; errors, validation of the picked file and how opening a project resets the other views aren't described.

less_defined.name: Git scope
less_defined.why: It says what git state exists and how fast it refreshes, but not how it's read, shared or cached, so each consumer polls git on its own.

less_defined.name: Application scope
less_defined.why: It gives the stack, name and platforms, but its list of .suspense contents leaves out several folders the app actually keeps (asks, divergence, system-prompts, commit notes).

less_defined.name: Code and Research ribbon tabs
less_defined.why: They're placeholders with no commands, so there's little to build or check.

less_defined.name: Spec library and agent definitions
less_defined.why: The abstract Concept/Scope/Shape anchors and the build skills/commands describe how the spec is organised and what the agent is told, not app behaviour, and they compile to the agent directory rather than src.

less_defined.name: Message list legibility
less_defined.why: The legibility section only asks for readable font sizes and colours, without values.
